tasks.short: Give blood products or infusions after bedside checks, monitor for adverse reactions and record the transfusion.

steps.what: Nurse checks the order, consent and blood group result in the record
Nurse collects the blood product or prepares the intravenous infusion
Nurse checks patient identity against the product at the bedside
Second nurse independently verifies patient, product and order
Nurse starts the blood transfusion or infusion and programs the pump
Nurse monitors patients for adverse reactions and takes vitals at set times
Nurse records times, product number and vitals in the transfusion record
Nurse stops for a reaction, informs the doctor and reports to the blood bank

tasks.design: Bedside barcode scanning of wristband, product label and nurse badge in the electronic health record ({OTHER}) speeds the identity checks, while the second nurse's independent verification stays. The pump takes its rate from the order, start and stop times and monitor vitals write into the transfusion record, and a reaction report is pre-filled from that record for the blood bank.
tasks.previous_blocker: Transfusion checks and records were paper-based protocols, and pumps and monitors were not linked to the record.
tasks.enabler_now: Bedside scanning, pump integration and monitor data feeds are standard options in hospital records.
tasks.still_hard: Spotting a reaction early is clinical vigilance; double-check rules come from protocol and cannot be skipped.
tasks.human_edge: Recognising the first signs of a reaction and stopping the transfusion in time.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; fewer handwritten entries and faster checks.

reach.task: Give transfusions with fewer staff around
reach.learn: Whether scanning plus a remote second check is acceptable under the protocol.

evidence.claim: Hospital records can link bedside barcode scans, infusion pumps and monitors to the medication and transfusion record.
The inspectorate names medication errors from wrong registration as a risk providers must manage.
Calamities must be reported to the inspectorate without delay; transfusion reactions also follow national reporting rules.

assumptions: Boundary: from checking the order to the transfusion recorded or a reaction reported; ordering and blood bank work are outside.
Input contract: barcoded wristbands from admission, product labels from the blood bank, nurse badges, physician orders in the record; fallback is the paper checklist.
The second independent check stays as hospital protocol requires.
Second nurse and physician time is outside this nurse's savings.
unknowns: Whether pumps and monitors are integrated with the record.
How many transfusions the unit gives per week.
research_questions: Do scanned checks reduce near misses in patient-product matching?

already_counted.description: Nurse checks the auto-recorded transfusion record before closing it.

incremental.description: Nurse resolves failed scans and pump-record mismatches.

approvals.approved_version: Product unit number matched to this patient's wristband and order at the bedside in s4; a different unit needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Units without pump and monitor integration keep manual recording; monitoring time does not change.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Take and read ECGs, check line and tube position on x-rays, compare with earlier results and alert the doctor.

steps.what: Nurse records a 12-lead ECG or prints a rhythm strip from the monitor
Nurse interprets the ECG: rhythm, rate, ST changes, intervals
Nurse checks line and tube position on the chest radiographs per protocol
Nurse finds and compares earlier ECGs in the record
Nurse informs the doctor of changes that need action
Intensivist confirms the interpretation and decides treatment

tasks.design: Configure the ECG management system linked to the record ({OTHER}) to open the patient's previous ECG beside the new one and show changes in the device's own measured intervals. Interpretation of ECGs and x-rays stays with the nurse and doctor; certified image-reading software is a separate decision for radiology, not assumed here.
tasks.previous_blocker: Earlier ECGs were found by scrolling through scans and paper strips.
tasks.enabler_now: ECG management systems store ECGs digitally and can show them side by side.
tasks.still_hard: Interpretation is clinical judgement with high stakes; AI reading would be a high-risk medical device.
tasks.human_edge: Linking an ECG change to the patient in front of them and calling the doctor at the right moment.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; comparison takes seconds.

reach.learn: Whether side-by-side comparison changes what they flag to nurses.

evidence.claim: Certified image-reading software flags findings on mammograms beside a radiologist.
Medical device software that needs a notified body brings AI Act high-risk duties.
ECG management systems can show a new ECG beside the previous one with measured differences.

assumptions: Boundary: from recording the ECG or opening the x-ray to the doctor's decision; treatment is outside.
Input contract: ECGs stored by the ECG devices in the ECG management system; x-rays in the imaging archive; fallback is searching the record.
The device's own interval measurements already exist and earn no saving.
Intensivist time is outside the nurse's savings.
unknowns: Whether older ECGs are stored digitally.
How often nurses compare ECGs per shift.
research_questions: Does side-by-side comparison change how often nurses alert the doctor?

already_counted.description: Nurse reviews the side-by-side comparison and measured changes.

incremental.description: Nurse reports ECGs filed under the wrong patient or time.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Units where earlier ECGs are seldom needed save almost nothing; interpretation is unchanged.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Handle the paperwork for admission, transfer and discharge: assessments, medication lists, bed requests and letters.

steps.what: Nurse receives the admission request and prepares the bed
Nurse completes the nursing admission assessment and forms
Nurse reconciles home medication with the pharmacy on admission
Pharmacist verifies the reconciled medication list
Nurse arranges the transfer: calls bed management and the receiving ward
Bed manager assigns a bed on the receiving ward
Nurse prepares transfer or discharge documents: letter, appointments, home care referral

loop.input: Structured record fields (diagnoses, medication, lines, wounds, mobility, allergies) and nursing reports of the stay.
loop.output: A nursing transfer or discharge letter in the receiving organisation's format.
loop.check: Structured sections are filled from fields, not the model; narrative lines must cite a report; medication and allergy sections must match the verified list word for word; the nurse signs before sending.
loop.stop: One draft and one retry; then the nurse writes the narrative.
loop.why_not_simpler: The narrative of the stay is spread over free-text reports; fields alone miss what the next team needs to know.

tasks.design: Admission forms in the electronic health record ({OTHER}) pre-fill from the emergency or theatre record and earlier admissions, and the home medication history is imported from the national exchange for reconciliation. Transfers go as requests in the bed management module, and transfer and discharge letters are built from fields plus a drafted narrative that the nurse checks and signs before sending.
tasks.previous_blocker: Admission and transfer data were re-typed between departments, and letters were written from scratch.
tasks.enabler_now: Records exchange data between departments and with community pharmacies, and letter drafting from the record is offered by Dutch scribe vendors.
tasks.still_hard: Medication reconciliation needs the pharmacist's check; summaries can miss things, and the inspectorate expects testing and monitoring.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing what the receiving nurse must hear about this patient and making sure nothing falls through the gap.

ambition.what: Every transfer and discharge with a complete letter at the moment the patient leaves.

tasks.altitude: The nurse checks and signs instead of typing; transfer decisions stay with doctors and bed management.

reach.task: Receive discharge letters for patients going home
reach.learn: Which letter sections home care actually uses.

evidence.claim: A Dutch scribe drafts referral letters and suggests codes; its owner's scribe and coding carry MDR class IIa.
Self-estimated time per note fell 29% across 236,153 scribe notes in a European health system.
Providers are responsible for careful use of generative AI, including testing and monitoring after updates.
The record is kept twenty years after the last change.

assumptions: Boundary: from the admission request to the patient transferred or discharged with documents; clinical care is outside.

Input contract: emergency and theatre records written by those teams; home medication from the national exchange; bed requests handled by bed managers in the bed module; fallback is phone and typed letters.
Drafting runs in the hospital's governed environment.
Pharmacist and bed manager time is outside the nurse's savings.
unknowns: Whether the record imports home medication automatically.
Number of transfers per day on the unit.
research_questions: Do receiving wards call back less often with generated letters?

already_counted.description: Nurse checks the pre-filled admission data.
Nurse checks and signs the drafted transfer or discharge letter.

incremental.description: Nurse reports letter errors and fixes wrong pre-filled data.
Clinical informatics audits letter samples and maintains templates.

approvals.approved_version: Transfer or discharge letter as signed by the nurse; any change after signing needs a new signature.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Units that still reconcile medication by phone and get many drafts that fail the check keep most paperwork time.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Assess pain and sedation, give drug and non-drug interventions, monitor responses and adjust the care plan.

steps.what: Nurse assesses pain and sedation with scores at set times
Nurse records the scores in the record
Nurse manages patients' pain relief and sedation: gives medication and adjusts pumps
Nurse applies non-drug interventions: positioning, cooling, reassurance
Nurse monitors responses and side effects such as breathing and blood pressure
Nurse discusses with the intensivist and changes care plans accordingly
Intensivist agrees changes to analgesia and sedation targets

tasks.design: Configure due-time prompts for pain and sedation scores at the bedside in the electronic health record ({OTHER}), show the hospital's approved protocol step for the current score next to the medication screen as a fixed lookup, and add a trend view of scores against doses and vital signs. The nurse decides every intervention; no software doses.
tasks.previous_blocker: Scores, doses and vitals were in separate screens, and protocols were on paper.
tasks.enabler_now: Records support bedside entry, due-time prompts and trend views as configuration.
tasks.still_hard: Pain and sedation management is continuous clinical judgement; dosing software would be a high-class medical device.
tasks.human_edge: Reading discomfort in a patient who cannot speak and balancing comfort against safety.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; scores and trends are at hand when deciding.

reach.learn: Whether the trend view fits recovery room handover.

evidence.claim: Decision-support software is usually MDR class IIa or higher, which a fixed protocol lookup avoids.
Solely automated decisions with significant effect need a specific legal basis; here the nurse decides.
Providers are responsible for careful use of new software in care.

assumptions: Boundary: from assessment to the care plan updated; prescribing by the intensivist is outside.
Input contract: scores entered by nurses at the bedside; approved sedation and pain protocol table maintained by the unit's protocol committee; vitals from monitors; fallback is the paper protocol.
The protocol lookup is fixed text tied to score bands, not a recommendation engine.
Intensivist time is outside the nurse's savings.
unknowns: Whether scores are entered at the bedside today.
Which pain and sedation scales the unit uses.
research_questions: Does a trend view change how quickly sedation is reduced?

incremental.description: Nurse answers due-time prompts that do not fit the patient's situation.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Units already scoring at the bedside save only on the trend view; clinical work does not change.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The acute care nurse keeps assessment, interventions and vigilance; recording, comparing and letters shift to checks and signatures.
skills_to_grow: Checking scanned and auto-recorded data quickly
Signing drafted letters with a critical eye
role.ambitious_version: An acute care nurse whose records complete themselves from devices and scans, leaving more time at the bedside.
